Coverage and enrichment testing

coverage_and_enrichment.Rmd

Overview

Among other things, the multifactor package provides a set of tools to calculate coverage and estimate enrichment for relational datasets. This type of operation forms the basis for bioinformatics techniques such as pathway enrichment analysis (PEA), but have application far beyond the biological sciences.

Setup 

library(multifactor)

# Wrangling
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)

# Plotting
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(ggforce)
library(systemfonts)
library(ragg)

# Define utility function
split_to_letters <- function(x) unique(
  unlist(
    strsplit(gsub(" ", "", x), split = ""),
    recursive = TRUE, use.names = FALSE
  )
)

Example Dataset: The Quick Brown Fox

We will use a toy data set of hierarchically structured data, namely the sentence: ‘The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.’ This sentence is a pangram, meaning that all 26 letters of the English alphabet are represented. Moreover, we have deconstructed the sentence to three levels; letters, words and constituents.

# Load the quick brown fox data set
set.seed(2612)
fox <- quickbrownfox()

We could represent these relations visually like so:

We can convince ourselves this same information is captured in the multifactor object, fox.

levels(fox)
#> $letter
#>  [1] "a" "b" "c" "d" "e" "f" "g" "h" "i" "j" "k" "l" "m" "n" "o" "p" "q" "r" "s"

#> 
#> $constituent
#> [1] "object"    "predicate" "subject"  
#> 
#> $sentence

as.matrix(fox$letter2word)

Calculate coverage

Introduction

With coverage, we mean the proportion of items in a set that are present. In other words, going back to our example, given some number of letters, we can calculate which words we can make, and how complete they are.

To demonstrate, let’s first consider the graph representation of our dataset:

Three feature types are shown on the x-axis, with links between respective levels as lines. We can see that each letter is linked to the words it appears in, which are in turn linked to their corresponding constituents.

We’ll also need to generate some collection of letters as input data:

# Generate some collection of letters
input <- split_to_letters("a pangram is a sentence with all letters")

input
#>  [1] "a" "p" "n" "g" "r" "m" "i" "s" "e" "t" "c" "w" "h" "l"

Defining coverage in a path

weave_coverage()

We can use the weave_coverage() function to calculate to what degree the input letters cover the words in our data set. This function behaves similarly to weave(), in the sense that it takes a multifactor as its first argument, x, and its second argument, .path, defines the path through that multifactor. It also has an additional argument, .data.

For now, let’s plug in our input letters:

res <- weave_coverage(
  x = fox, .path = letter ~ word ~ constituent, .data = input
)

Filter using subset()

We can use the subset() method for linkmap to automatically filter for complete cases, only the word ‘the’ is complete:

subset(res)
#> A multifactor::linkmap data.frame S7_object: 0 rows.
#> [1] letter      constituent
#> <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)
#> 
#> @ levels:   2 variables: 
#>  $ letter      : 26 Levels: a ... z 
#>  $ constituent :  3 Levels: object predicate subject

By default, coverage is only calculated between the data types involved in the last step of the path. However, we can specify conditional filtering steps.

Complete coverage

When defining a path, we can use the : operator as shorthand for complete coverage (>= 1). For example: letter ~ word ~ constituent >= 1 is equivalent to letter ~ word : constituent.

weave_coverage(
  x = fox, .path = letter ~ word : constituent, .data = input
)
#> A multifactor::linkmap data.frame S7_object: 0 rows.
#> [1] letter      constituent
#> <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)
#> 
#> @ levels:   2 variables: 
#>  $ letter      : 26 Levels: a ... z 
#>  $ constituent :  3 Levels: object predicate subject

Partial coverage

We can similarly define threshold-based filters using relational expressions. For example: letter ~ word > 0.5 ~ constituent is equivalent to letter ~ word : constituent.

weave_coverage(
  x = fox, .path = letter ~ word > 0.5 ~ constituent, .data = input
)
#> A multifactor::linkmap data.frame S7_object: 34 rows.
#>    letter constituent
#> 1       a      object
#> 2       d      object
#> 3       e      object
#> 4       g      object
#> 5       h      object
#> 6       l      object
#> 7       o      object
#> 8       t      object
#> 9       y      object
#> 10      z      object
#>  + 24 more rows. Use `print(n = ...)` to see more rows.
#> 
#> @ levels:   2 variables: 
#>  $ letter      : 26 Levels: a ... z 
#>  $ constituent :  3 Levels: object predicate subject 
#> 
#> @ metadata: 5 variables: 
#> List of 5
#>  $ set_size : int  10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 ...
#>  $ observed : logi  FALSE FALSE TRUE FALSE TRUE FALSE ...
#>  $ set_count: int  3 3 3 3 3 3 3 3 3 3 ...
#>  $ coverage : num  0.3 0.3 0.3 0.3 0.3 0.3 0.3 0.3 0.3 0.3 ...
#>  $ complete : logi  FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE ...

Enrichment testing

The test_enrich() allows for quick hypothesis testing using the same syntax:

test_enrich(x = fox, .path = letter ~ word, .data = input)
#>        expected  observed      fold   log_fold   p.value p.adj
#> brown 0.5384615 0.6000000 1.1142857  0.1561192 0.5782609     1
#> dog   0.5384615 0.3333333 0.6190476 -0.6918777 0.9153846     1
#> fox   0.5384615 0.0000000 0.0000000       -Inf 1.0000000     1
#> jumps 0.5384615 0.6000000 1.1142857  0.1561192 0.5782609     1
#> lazy  0.5384615 0.5000000 0.9285714 -0.1069152 0.7608696     1
#> over  0.5384615 0.5000000 0.9285714 -0.1069152 0.7608696     1
#> quick 0.5384615 0.4000000 0.7428571 -0.4288433 0.8826087     1
#> the   0.5384615 1.0000000 1.8571429  0.8930848 0.1400000     1

Alternatively, test_enrich() can also be run on the result of an earlier weave_coverage() call for the same results:

test_enrich(res)
#>            expected  observed      fold    log_fold   p.value     p.adj
#> object    0.5384615 0.6000000 1.1142857  0.15611920 0.4640194 0.6759052
#> predicate 0.5384615 0.5555556 1.0317460  0.04508789 0.6132723 0.6759052
#> subject   0.5384615 0.5333333 0.9904762 -0.01380580 0.6759052 0.6759052
